newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Major lauds Bangladesh's efforts for investment.
newsitem.headline: Major lauds Bangladesh's efforts for investment.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, after a whirlwind tour of India which saw him mobbed by well-wishers and feted by the media, praised Bangladesh on Saturday for its efforts to attract foreign investment.
But he said there were still steps the government must take to eliminate the bureaucracy and obstacles to trade.
"I hope you will continue to apply your scissors ruthlessly to the red tape," Major told businessmen in Dhaka in the keynote speech of his one-day stay in Bangladesh.

Major, leaving at home a desperate race by his ruling Conservative Party to overhaul the opposition Labour Party before a general election, held talks earlier on Saturday with Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.
Major was also due to meet opposition leader Begum Khaleda Zia on Saturday.
He toured rural areas where he announced around four million pounds in new development aid for health and education projects.
Major also witnessed the signing of a $150 million contract between Petrobangla and Britain's Cairn Energy to jointly develop the Sangu offshore gas field in the Bay of Bengal.
The first gas is due to come on stream in 1998.
The visit is the second leg of a south Asian tour that will also take the British leader to Pakistan.

Major has been privately criticised at home by nervous members of parliament from his party for scheduling a week-long foreign trip at a crucial time in the run-up to a general election, now no more than four months away.
But Major, unfazed by an opposition Labour Party opinion poll lead of some 20 points, has rejected such criticism, saying he remains Britain's leader and his job is to boost trade.
But domestic politics were never far away on his last scheduled foreign trip before the election.

News that the Conservatives will call a by-election in an English parliamentary seat left vacant by the death of a Conservative member, despite the likelihood it will lose, provoked immediate speculation about the general election date.
Major denied to reporters that he had given up hope of seeing out his full term, suggesting May 1 was still his preferred election date. The last possible date is May 22.
Aides sought to refocus the media'a attention on the successes of the trip, designed to open doors and forge long-term commercial links.
Major is due to travel on Sunday to Pakistan, where he will hold talks with government and opposition leaders as well as travel to the Khyber Pass, the legendary gateway to the subcontinent.
Bangldesh was part of India under British rule between 1772 and 1947. It became independent in 1971.
